newsitem.title: USA: Albright sees China concerns, Russia initiative.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees China concerns, Russia initiative.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright has expressed deep concerns about Chinese arms sales and expects a new initiative for ex-Soviet states, according to documents recently made available by a Senate panel.
The information was provided in written answers to more than 200 questions posed by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee as part of Albright's confirmation process.
The panel, which held a public hearing last week, voted unanimously on Monday to support her appointment. The full Senate is expected formally to confirm her on Wednesday.

In the documents, examined by Reuters, Albright said "We are deeply troubled with respect to Chinese missile cooperation with Pakistan and Iran and transfers by Chinese entities of dual-use chemicals and equipment to Iran."
But Albright said there was no evidence current Chinese activities regarding arms transfers merit U.S. sanctions.
The administration is unaware of "any credible evidence" that Chinese companies are assisting biological warfare programs in Iraq, Syria or Libya, she said.

But she noted what the State Department acknowledged last November, that "we have received reporting regarding transfers of dual-use (biological-related) items from Chinese entities to Iranian government entities which raise concern."

She recalled that in 1993, Washington imposed sanctions on Chinese entities for selling missile-related equipment to Pakistan, and insisted: "If we determine that Chinese transfers trigger our laws, we will impose sanctions again."
She promised to monitor the situation and continue to make stopping the spread of destabilizing arms a top priority.

Albright talked tough on trade, asserting the need for "up-front commitments from China to expand market access significantly for our exporters and investors as part of" Beijing's bid for membership in the World Trade Organization.
This includes persuading China to liberalize its trading rights regime and comply with the WTO agreement on subsidies.
Washington backs Beijing's bid to join the WTO but has insisted the terms be similar to developed nations, not the easier criteria of developing nations, as China has demanded.
Albright also said "we have no intention of exempting China from our anti-dumping laws."

On Hong Kong, which is due to return to Beijing's control on July 1, she said China's decision to replace the current elected legislative council with a provisional legislature was "both unjustified and unnecessary."
"Beijing's decision raises questions about Hong Kong's future autonomy and China's intention to implement the commitments it has made," she said.
She noted "a provisional legislature also obviously does not reflect the representative will of the Hong Kong people" and promised to watch the situation closely.
Albright disclosed that the administration plans an initiative designed to move ex-Soviet states, especially Russia, from economic stability to economic growth.
Stressing that one critical U.S. national security interest in the next four years is the future of the former Soviet Union's newly independent states, she said:

"We will seek funding for a new Partnership for Freedom initiative, the centerpiece of which is a package of measures built to move the NIS, particularly Russia, from economic stability to economic growth."

Albright said this initiative, to be outlined in President Bill Clinton's 1998 budget due out soon, would concentrate on trade, investment and anti-crime programs, as well as environment and energy." She gave no more details.
In addition, Albright:

-- endorsed maintaining aid to Israel at the current level of $3 billion a year, -- indicated Iran policy would not change, saying: "Our commitment to containing Iran remains firm. There is currently no formal review of U.S. policy toward Iran under way or planned."
